Insatiable

/in-SAY-shuh-buhl/ - the stress falls on SAY · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Insatiable means incapable of being satisfied.

No matter how many thrillers the library buys, Mr. Okafor's insatiable reading appetite clears the new-arrivals shelf by Friday.

Worked Example

Forty years in, the map collector's hunger is unchanged: each new atlas satisfies him for exactly one evening. By breakfast the wanting is back, pointing at a gap on the shelf only he can see. His spouse stopped asking 'how many is enough?' decades ago — with him, there is no number.

Insatiable is built to say exactly this: in- (not) + satis (enough) — no amount is ever enough. A big appetite can be met with a big meal, and a vast collection can, given years enough, be finished. Insatiable removes the finish line altogether; the wanting always outlives the getting.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

unquenchable: no drink puts it out — the word for thirsts, of the body and of the mind

ravenous: fiercely hungry right now; a feast can cure it

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

contented: wanting nothing more than what's already there

temperate: keeping every appetite firmly in check

Where it sits · how long the appetite survives feeding — eager → ravenous → insatiable

eager vs. insatiable: Eager wants keenly and waits politely; insatiable wants without end — feeding it only sharpens it.

ravenous vs. insatiable: Ravenous is hunger at full roar, but even a ravenous crew is quiet after two pots of stew; insatiable outlasts every serving you bring.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-

Prefix — in-: not

Root — sati-

Root — sati-: enough (Latin satis)

Suffix — -able

Suffix — -able: able to be

Put it together

Put it together: In- (not) + sati- (enough — Latin satis) + -able = not able to be given enough. Latin satis is the ancestor of a small family of fullness words, and insatiable is its negation walking upright: a hunger built so that 'enough' never arrives.

Use the root in a new word: satisfy

Use the root in a new word: satisfy: A single square of chocolate, oddly, satisfies her completely.

Word Choice

neutral / literary

Insatiable describes the hunger, not the meal — curiosity, drive, an audience's demand — and insists no amount will end it. Gluttony, its unit-mate, judges the behavior at the table: indulging past fullness. A glutton overshoots 'enough'; the insatiable never meet it. Keep the vice with the food and insatiable with the endless wanting.
